en: The Sūtra on the Mallas Moving the Mountain, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of India during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the kingdom of Kuśinagara, at the birthplace of the Mallas.
In a great grove of trees, he was together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, the ministers and citizens of the kingdom all came forth to assemble.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"For what reason has the great assembly of this country gathered like clouds?
The worthy Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"Not far from here stands a great rocky mountain, sixty *zhang* square and one hundred and twenty *zhang* high, which blocks the path and hinders those who travel. Five hundred men of great strength deliberated together, saying:

'Our physical might is praised throughout the world as rare; it would be a waste to merely maintain this strength without benefit to the times. We should join forces to move it and establish a merit for future generations.'"

They immediately joined their strength and raised their voices in a chorus of cries; though they were exhausted by their own efforts and unable to move it, the sound reverberated far and wide, and thus the people of the village flocked together to witness the spectacle.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Adjust your dharma robes and proceed with solemnity to observe him.

Having received these instructions, Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and followed alone as an attendant, walking behind the Buddha in a protective and reverent manner.
The great assembly of five hundred strongmen beheld from afar the arrival of the Buddha;
his golden countenance was composed, his majestic radiance was towering and sublime, his appearance was upright and exquisite, and his physical form was pure.
Adorned with the marks and signs of a Great Being, he had subdued the elements of the aggregates and was free from the influxes; his mind was profoundly serene and his faculties were tranquil.
In meditative concentration (*samādhi*), harmonious, joyful, tranquil, and profound, he is the foremost among gods and humans. His great radiance is brilliant and majestic;
he shines like a mountain of jewels, as luminous as a great torch that illuminates the dark and obscure.
He is like a great mountain ridge with accumulated snow, like the light of the sun rising at dawn, and like the full autumn moon standing out among the multitude of stars.
His brilliance was like that of a Wheel-Turning King accompanied by his various precious ministers and the fourfold assembly;
like trees and flowers in full bloom, it was magnificent and luxuriant, its peerless splendor far surpassing his own person.

A multitude of five hundred strongmen and countless others gazed upon these divine transformations; none failed to leap for joy as virtuous thoughts arose within them one after another. They came forward to receive him, prostrating themselves with their five limbs to bow their heads at his feet, and with single-minded reverence, they withdrew to stand to one side.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One asked the Mallas,
"For what reason are your bodies exhausted and your complexions haggard?
They replied:

"This great rock is sixty zhang square and one hundred twenty zhang high; we wished to lift and move it together, but from the first day of our diligent exertion until the end of the month, it could not be moved at all. Ashamed of our lack of efficacy and ridiculed by the world, we are thus utterly exhausted and our complexions have grown haggard."
"What do you hope for here?
The Malla replied,
"Indeed, Great Sage!"

My power of merit is such that none can surpass it; I hope, therefore, to move this stone to bring further benefit to the world, establishing my name and perpetuating my achievements so that future generations may record my fame, and thereby making the royal road level and straight, causing even the remote regions to submit and return to allegiance.
The Buddha told the Mallas:
"I understand that your compassionate intent is beyond your capacity; I shall move it for you so as to fulfill your original vow, enabling you to bear this merit without shame or fear."
The Malla, filled with joy, replied, "I respectfully obey.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One adjusted his dharma robes and, using the big toe of his right foot, lifted the mountain rock and tossed it up to the Brahma Heaven. He caught it in his right palm, squeezed it three times, and placed it in the void at a height of four *zhang* and nine *chi* above the ground. Returning it to his palm, he crushed it into fine shavings between three fingers and blew them away until they were completely dissolved. At that moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.

At that time, when the Mallas saw the Buddha’s supernatural transformations and majestic spiritual power manifesting, they were immediately seized with awe and fear, their hair standing on end, and they said to the World-Honored One:
"Is this movement of the fingers the result of the power of the Great Sage’s parents who nurtured him with milk?"
"Is it the power of the divine feet, wisdom, or the mental formations?
He replied, "It is the force of nursing; it is not due to any other power."

If I were to exercise my power of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi*), I could take this trichiliocosm, the world-system of the Buddha, and lift it up to place it in hundreds of thousands of other extraordinary buddha-fields, yet without causing anyone to have any perception of coming or going, nor endangering sentient beings, nor harming the insects of the earth.
The Malla asked again,
"What is the appearance of the strength derived from nursing?
The World-Honored One replied:
"One hundred oxen equal the strength of one water buffalo;
one hundred water buffaloes equal the strength of one blue ox;
one hundred blue oxen equal the strength of one gayal."
A hundred *ṛṣabha* oxen equal the strength of one *veṇu* ox;
a hundred *veṇu* oxen equal the strength of one *tṛṇa* elephant;
a hundred *tṛṇa* elephants equal the strength of one ordinary elephant.
One hundred ordinary elephants equal the strength of one black elephant;
one hundred black elephants equal the strength of one white elephant;
one hundred white elephants equal the strength of one dragon.
A hundred times the strength of a dragon is equal to one unit of the strength of a formidable wrestler;
a hundred times the strength of a formidable wrestler is equal to one unit of the strength of a segment-wrestler;
a hundred times the strength of a segment-wrestler is equal to one unit of the strength of a collapsing-wrestler.
One hundred units of the strength of a *bhaṅga* wrestler equal one unit of the strength of a *mahābhaṅga* wrestler;
one hundred units of the strength of a *mahābhaṅga* wrestler equal one unit of the strength of a *ardhapauruṣa* wrestler;
and one hundred units of the strength of an *ardhapauruṣa* wrestler equal one unit of the strength of a *pauruṣa* wrestler.
The strength of one hundred strongmen of the human vehicle is equal to the strength of one strongman of the Great Man vehicle;
yet even that infinite strength does not equal the strength of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, at the time of suckling from his mother’s breast.
The Buddha told the Mallas:
"You should know that this is the strength of the Tathāgata from his infancy.
The Mallas addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The Great Sage has already manifested the power of suckling; what then is his power of supernormal faculties?
The Buddha told the Mallas:
“Recall that in the past, when I was traveling through various kingdoms together with Mahāmaudgalyāyana, there was a famine and the community of bhikṣus was unable to obtain alms.”
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:

“Grain has soared in price and the people are starving. Now, when the bhikṣus go on their alms-rounds, they obtain nothing; their physical strength has declined and they are unable to recite the scriptures. Day by day they grow more emaciated, and I fear they will not survive.”

In ancient times, when heaven and earth first came into being, the earth produced the natural flavor of ambrosia; those who consumed it were healthy and peaceful, and their four elements were at ease. Later, as the merit of people grew thin, the flavor vanished into the earth.

"Now I wish to return to the earth to bring forth the flavors of antiquity, so that the bhikṣus and the people of the land may all obtain their lives and be fully satiated, enabling them to recite the sūtras and contemplate the Way.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: "Desist!"

If one were to overturn the earth, the insects, moths, and other wriggling creatures dwelling therein would surely be harmed; furthermore, as the merit of the multitude is meager, they ought not to consume the flavor of the ancient earth.
Maudgalyāyana spoke again:
"I shall take these bhikṣus and the emaciated, starving people to the land of Uttarakuru, so that they may partake of the naturally grown non-glutinous rice."
The World-Honored One said, "Those who possess the power of supernormal travel (ṛddhi) can reach it by themselves; how could one who has not yet attained the ability for light flight go there?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"Those who lack supernatural power, I shall support and escort so that they may attain peace.

Such was the majestic transformative power of Maudgalyāyana’s virtue. Calculatedly, Jambudvīpa is twenty-eight thousand li in breadth and length; its land is broad at the top and narrow at the bottom.
Aparagoyānī is thirty-two thousand li in breadth and length; its land resembles the shape of a half-moon.
The realm of Aparagoyānī is thirty-six hundred thousand li in breadth and length; its terrain is perfectly circular.
The realm of Uttarakuru is forty thousand li in breadth and length; its terrain is perfectly square.
Mountains encircle it on all sides to form the four quarters of the realm.

Suppose all the people therein were to attain supernormal powers like those of Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and each one were to fill the trichiliocosm; yet they would not equal the Tathāgata’s supernormal power by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, or even a trillionfold. Even calculating it as empty space, there is nothing to which it can be compared; this is the supernormal power of the Tathāgata.
The Malla further addressed him, saying:
"Great Sage!
You have already manifested the power of suckling and the power of supernormal feats; we pray that you will now further manifest the power of wisdom."
The World-Honored One replied:

"It is reckoned that the great ocean is three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li* deep, its breadth and length being beyond measure. Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, stands within this great ocean; it is three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li* high, and its base beneath the ocean floor is likewise three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li*, with its dimensions in each direction being the same."
One might drink up all the waters of the great ocean until nothing remains; yet the wisdom of Śāriputra cannot be measured, and there is no one capable of diminishing it.

Suppose the realms of the four directions were filled with people, and each were made to possess wisdom equal to that of Śāriputra, such that they individually overflowed the trichiliocosm—this would not compare to the power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom by even a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, or a trillionfold. Even calculating through emptiness, it cannot be compared, for there is no metaphor by which it can be illustrated. This is the power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
The Malla again addressed him:
"Great Sage!
You have already manifested the powers of suckling, supernormal feats, and wisdom; we pray that you will further manifest the power of mental action."

The World-Honored One said: "Suppose clouds arise and fill the four quarters, and a great rain falls everywhere throughout the trichiliocosm. Regarding the places from which the rain originates and the paths it traverses—whether it be stalks, joints, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits; whether it be water in vessels, mountains, stones, grass, or reeds; or the various classes of beings, crawling, breathing, or human—all the individual drops, whether large or small, return to the great ocean. The Tathāgata can distinguish and track each one to name them, and he recognizes and refines them all, returning them to their original state without error. The power of the Tathāgata’s mind knows and understands all this without any obstruction; this is the Tathāgata’s power of mental activity."
The Malla again addressed him, saying:
"Great Sage!
You have already manifested the powers of suckling, supernormal feats, wisdom, and mental conduct; is there yet another power that surpasses these?"
The World-Honored One said:

“The strength of the Tathāgata’s nursing, the power of Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal feats, the power of Śāriputra’s wisdom, and the power of the mental conduct of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not compare to the ten powers of the Tathāgata, which are vast, far-reaching, and limitless.”
The Malla asked, “What are the ten powers?
The World-Honored One replied:

"To clearly perceive all things—whether subtle or manifest, distant or near, heterodox or orthodox, whether they pertain to this place or not, and whether they are finite or infinite—and to know them all with precise clarity as they truly are: this is the first power."
Regarding all places of retribution experienced throughout the past, future, and present, he knows them all with clear and precise certainty; this is the second power.
Regarding meditative concentration, right reception, and the three gates of liberation, he knows them all with clear and precise certainty; this is the third power.

To behold that the fundamental nature of the minds of all sentient beings is inherently pure and there is nothing they do not understand, and to know them all with clear and precise discernment as they truly are—this is the fourth power.

To comprehend the various kinds of speech of all classes of beings, their differing mental inclinations, and their diverse physical forms, and to know them all with clear and precise discernment as they truly are—this is the fifth power.
He discerns the various and immeasurable dispositions of the multitude of beings, each distinct; knowing them all with clear and precise certainty as they truly are—this is the sixth power.

His wisdom is like the ocean and his eloquence is immeasurable; he recollects all that has been experienced in past lives, knowing it all with clear and precise certainty as it truly was—this is the seventh power.

He clearly understands the essentials of binding by desire and liberation from bondage; wherever he goes, he acts in accordance with circumstances, administering medicine according to the ailment. With the divine eye, he perceives the good and evil, the beginnings and ends, and the destinations of calamity and fortune for all people. Examining them with clarity and precision as they truly are, he knows them all completely—this is the eighth power.

The Path possesses the power of hearing with penetrating clarity; it understands all sounds of devas and humans, and there is no sound of crawling, breathing, or wriggling creatures that it does not comprehend. It knows them all as they truly exist, clearly and distinctly; this is the ninth power.

The Buddha is free from all outflows (*āsrava*), his beginning and end are forever exhausted, and he is no longer bound by attachment. With a divine, true, and sagely wisdom, he personally realizes and witnesses [the truth]; he has thoroughly mastered the practice of the Way, accomplished what was to be done, and is beyond further birth and death. He beholds the fundamental nature of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, perceiving everything without exception; he examines them with clarity and precision, knowing them exactly as they are—this is the Ten Powers (*daśabala*).
The Mallas addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Great Sage!
You have already manifested the power of suckling, supernormal powers, wisdom, mental activity, and the ten powers; is there yet any further distinction that surpasses all other powers?”
The World-Honored One replied:

"Though all other powers may be exceedingly strong—hundredfold, thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, or even hundred-millionfold—the power of impermanence is reckoned as the most supreme, for it subdues and overcomes them all."

Why is this? The body of the Tathāgata is of the nature of adamant; impermanence shall overcome me, and it must eventually fall into decay. This very night, at midnight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa at the place where the Mallas were born. At the crossroads, one should make offerings to my śarīra and erect stūpas and temples.

Why is this? Because people from the four quarters bring various flowers and incense, set up banners and streamers, hang silk pennants, bells, and canopies, and offer lamps; all these are directed toward the truly wondrous Dharma.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"All phenomena that arise must come to an end; That which prospers shall inevitably decline.
All things are impermanent; To contemplate this is true peace."
To obtain hundreds of thousands of golden mountains, with blessings and fortune beyond compare,
is not as good as offering clay stupas and joyfully returning to a sublime monastery.
To acquire hundreds of thousands of treasuries of jewels, with auspicious merit beyond calculation, is likewise surpassed by this.
It is not as good as making offerings at a mud stupa, Rejoicing and leaping as one returns to a superior temple.
Even if one were to provide hundreds of thousands of jeweled chariots, Carrying those of a complexion like purple-gold,
It is not as good as making offerings at an earthen temple, Leaping for joy and taking refuge in the Buddha.

When the Buddha spoke this sutra, the assembly of five hundred Mallas realized that the world is impermanent and that the three realms are unreliable; they understood that there is no single true reality other than the Dharma upon which one may rely. Their arrogance was immediately dispelled and they ceased to conceive of a self. They all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, and at that moment, they all established themselves on the stage of non-retrogression.
There were hundreds of thousands of countless devas and humans who, having distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attained the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, there was none who did not rejoice; each bowed their head to the ground to pay homage to the Buddha.
The Sūtra on the Mallas Moving the Mountain Spoken by the Buddha
